name: Naltrexone (Vivitrol, ReVia)
summary: Opioid receptor blocker used in addiction psychiatry to reduce alcohol cravings and prevent opioid relapse. It’s not a sedative and won’t get you “high,” but it can be dangerous if opioids are in your system.
description: Naltrexone helps with alcohol use disorder by turning down the “reward” signal from drinking, which can reduce cravings and heavy-drinking days. For opioid use disorder, it works by blocking opioid receptors—so opioids won’t work (and trying to override the block can be fatal). The biggest rules: you must be opioid-free before starting, you need liver monitoring, and you need a plan for pain control and surgery because opioid pain meds may not work while you’re on it.
patient_summary: Naltrexone is a non-addictive medication used in addiction treatment. It can reduce alcohol cravings and helps prevent opioid relapse by blocking opioid receptors. You MUST be opioid-free before starting or it can trigger sudden withdrawal. Don’t test the “block” with opioids—overdose risk goes up, especially near the end of the monthly injection or after stopping.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Opioid Antagonist (mu receptor antagonist; also blocks kappa/delta)

primary_indications: Opioid Use Disorder (relapse prevention / opioid blockade)

linked_conditions.context: Used to reduce cravings and cut down heavy-drinking days. Can be started even if the person is still drinking, as long as they’re not in dangerous withdrawal and there are no major contraindications.

Works by blocking opioid effects. Requires a verified opioid-free period before starting to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Best fit for people who are highly motivated, have reliable follow-up, and want a non-agonist option.
Sometimes used as part of combination treatment (commonly paired with bupropion) in specialized addiction care. It’s not a magic switch—think “modest help,” not “instant cure.”

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to naltrexone or any component of the formulation
Current use of opioid analgesics (including partial agonists)
Failure to pass a naloxone challenge test or positive opioid screen when opioid-free status is uncertain
Acute hepatitis or hepatic failure (noted in Canadian labeling; commonly treated as a major safety stop sign clinically)

efficacy_response.metric: Prevention of return to heavy drinking (oral naltrexone 50 mg/day in trials)
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Compared with placebo in a large systematic review of alcohol pharmacotherapy trials
efficacy_response.patient_text: Translation: it’s a real effect, but not a miracle. For about every 11 people treated, 1 additional person avoids returning to heavy drinking compared with placebo. The bigger win is often fewer “blowout” nights and less compulsive drinking.

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Oral: variable (~5% to 40%) due to first-pass metabolism
pharmacokinetics.onset: Oral: ~30 to 60 minutes (receptor blockade begins quickly)
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral: ~60 minutes; IM: biphasic peaks (~2 hours and ~2 to 3 days)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Oral naltrexone: ~4 hours; active metabolite (6-beta-naltrexol): ~13 hours; IM formulation: effective half-life depends on polymer erosion (naltrexone/metabolite ~5 to 10 days)
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Oral: 50 mg blocks receptors ~24 hours; higher doses can extend blockade (clinical effect varies by person)
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: IM: designed for ~4 weeks of coverage
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism (non-CYP pathways) to 6-beta-naltrexol and other metabolites; glucuronidation occurs
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily urine (mostly metabolites; small amounts unchanged)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken with or without food; taking with food may reduce nausea

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Naltrexone is used in addiction psychiatry for alcohol use disorder and opioid use disorder. It’s not a benzo, not a sedative, and it’s not habit-forming. Think of it as a “reward blocker” (alcohol) and a “receptor shield” (opioids).
items: {link:condition:alcohol-use-disorder:Alcohol Use Disorder (moderate to severe)}: Helps reduce cravings and heavy drinking
{link:condition:opioid-use-disorder:Opioid Use Disorder}: Prevents opioid effects and helps reduce relapse risk after detox
Relapse prevention: A protective layer when the plan is long-term recovery plus therapy/support
off_label: Methamphetamine use disorder (typically as part of combination treatment in specialty care)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: People don’t usually describe naltrexone as a “feeling” medication. It’s more like: you notice what doesn’t happen.

quotes: I could drink, but it just didn’t hit the same.
The cravings got quieter—like the urge wasn’t running the show anymore.
I stopped chasing that “buzz,” because it wasn’t paying off.

items.category: Opioids don’t work (and that’s the point)
quotes: It felt like a safety lock. I knew using wouldn’t do what it used to do.
I stopped fantasizing about relapse because I knew it wouldn’t ‘work.’
I had to grieve the idea of opioids—because the medication made the fantasy pointless.
items.note: Trying to override the blockade is one of the fastest ways to end up in an overdose situation.

items.category: Early side effects (usually the first days to weeks)
quotes: Nausea was the main thing at first.
Headache and this ‘blah’ feeling for a bit.
My sleep got weird for a week or two, then settled.
items.note: Side effects tend to be front-loaded—worse early, better later.

quotes: The shot site hurt for a couple days—worth it for the convenience.
I liked not having a daily pill decision.
I was paranoid about a lump at the injection site, but it went down.
items.note: Injection technique matters a lot. Deep IM in the glute is not optional.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Naltrexone starts blocking receptors quickly, but the real-life benefit (cravings and behavior) can take time to show up consistently.
key_points: Oral: ~30 to 60 minutes to reach peak levels and start meaningful receptor blockade
Oral: blockade duration is dose-dependent (50 mg is often described as ~24 hours of blockade coverage)
IM (Vivitrol): starts with an early peak around ~2 hours, then a second peak ~2 to 3 days later
IM: designed for coverage for about 4 weeks (monthly dosing)
If you stop it: overdose risk can rise because tolerance drops and sensitivity can rebound

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Reduced risk of returning to heavy drinking (oral naltrexone 50 mg/day)
sections.text: Across clinical trials, oral naltrexone shows a modest but meaningful benefit in alcohol use disorder, especially for reducing heavy-drinking relapse. The biggest “feel it in real life” wins are fewer binges, less compulsive drinking, and more ability to pause and choose.
sections.clinical_details: In a large systematic review of adult alcohol use disorder trials, oral naltrexone 50 mg/day was associated with lower rates of return to heavy drinking compared with placebo, with an estimated number needed to treat around 11. Effects vary: it tends to work best when paired with therapy, structure, and clear goals (reduce vs abstain).

citation.title: Pharmacotherapy for Alcohol Use Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: If opioids are in your system, naltrexone can trigger sudden withdrawal. And if you try to override the opioid block, you can overdose and die.
other: Opioid-free requirement: Do not start until you are opioid-free (including tramadol). A medically supervised start is recommended when opioid status is uncertain.
Precipitated withdrawal: Can begin within minutes, peak within 1 to 3 hours, and can be intense for 48 to 72 hours if opioids are still on board.
Accidental overdose risk: Overdose risk can increase near the end of the injection interval, after missed doses, or after stopping—because tolerance drops and receptor sensitivity can shift.
Liver risk: Can raise liver enzymes; hepatitis has been reported, especially with higher oral doses or in people with liver disease risk factors.
Depression/suicidality: Depression, suicidal thoughts, and attempted suicide have been reported postmarketing—monitor mood closely.
Injection-site injury (IM): Incorrect administration can cause severe tissue injury, abscess, necrosis, and rare Nicolau syndrome.
patient_counseling: Do not take any opioids while on naltrexone. This includes pain pills, some cough meds, and ‘just one’ from someone else’s stash.
Do not “test the block.” Trying to override naltrexone with large opioid doses is a recipe for overdose.
Tell every clinician you see that you’re on naltrexone—especially before surgery or dental work.
If you need planned surgery with possible opioid pain meds: oral naltrexone is typically stopped at least 72 hours beforehand; the IM shot requires planning about a month ahead.
Call your prescriber if you develop severe abdominal pain, dark urine, yellow eyes/skin, or unusually bad fatigue—those can be liver warning signs.
If you feel depressed, hopeless, or suicidal, treat that like an emergency—reach out immediately.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common issues are nausea, headache, dizziness, insomnia/sleep disturbance, and injection-site reactions with Vivitrol. Most side effects are worst early and improve over time.
plain_language_list: Injection-site pain, swelling, lumps, itching (IM formulation)
Liver enzyme elevations (usually mild, sometimes serious)

common.incidence: Up to ~33% (reported with IM formulation in labeling)
common.patient_note: This is the classic early side effect. Taking oral naltrexone with food can help. It often fades after the first couple of weeks.
Annoying but usually manageable. If it’s severe or persistent, your prescriber should reassess dosing and other causes.
Some people feel wired or sleep gets choppy at first. If sleep is already fragile, plan for this and tighten sleep hygiene early.
This isn’t a calming medication. If anxiety spikes, it may be withdrawal-related (from substances), stress-related, or a medication side effect—don’t guess, evaluate.

common.incidence: Very common (reported as high frequency in labeling; includes nodules, swelling, induration, tenderness, pain, pruritus)
common.patient_note: Expect soreness and a lump sometimes. Severe redness, worsening pain, drainage, fever, or skin breakdown is not normal—get evaluated fast.

common.incidence: Variable; increases are reported (often mild and transient)
common.patient_note: This is why baseline and periodic liver tests matter—especially if you have hepatitis C, HIV, heavy alcohol use, or are taking other liver-stressing meds.

serious: Naltrexone-precipitated opioid withdrawal: rapid onset (minutes), severe symptoms, sometimes requiring hospitalization.
Accidental opioid overdose: especially after stopping, missing doses, near the end of the injection interval, or attempting to override blockade.
Hepatitis / severe liver injury: marked enzyme elevation, jaundice, systemic symptoms.
Severe injection-site reactions: abscess, cellulitis, hematoma, tissue necrosis; rare Nicolau syndrome.
Depression, suicidal thoughts, suicide attempts (postmarketing reports): requires close monitoring and urgent intervention when present.
Seizure (rare, reported): evaluate for other causes and substance-related factors.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: The main interaction story is simple: opioids and naltrexone do not mix. Beyond that, watch the liver and be smart about combination regimens.

items.with: Opioids (including partial agonists and opioid-containing products)
items.risk: Blocks opioid effects and can precipitate severe withdrawal if opioids are in the body. Attempts to override blockade increase overdose and death risk.
items.action: AVOID opioids while on naltrexone. Verify opioid-free status before starting. Make a pain plan before surgery or dental work.

items.with: Planned or emergency opioid pain management
items.risk: Opioids may be ineffective; high-dose attempts can be dangerous. Pain control becomes complicated.
items.action: Use non-opioid strategies when possible (regional anesthesia, non-opioid analgesics, general anesthesia strategies). If opioids are required, care should be under trained anesthesia/acute pain specialists.

items.with: Other hepatotoxic agents (including heavy alcohol use and frequent NSAID use)
items.risk: Higher risk of liver enzyme elevation or hepatitis when the liver is already stressed.
items.action: Check baseline liver tests and monitor periodically. Reassess if symptoms of liver injury appear.

items.with: Bupropion (when used in combination approaches for stimulant use disorder)
items.risk: Combination can be activating for some patients (anxiety/insomnia). Bupropion also carries seizure risk in vulnerable patients.
items.action: If using combination therapy, monitor sleep, anxiety, blood pressure, and seizure risk factors. Adjust timing and dosing to reduce activation.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Naltrexone does not require a taper. But stopping it is not “no big deal” in addiction care—because relapse and overdose risk can change after discontinuation.
key_points: No taper needed: You can stop oral or IM naltrexone without tapering.
Overdose risk warning: After stopping, opioid tolerance can be lower than you remember. Using “your old dose” can kill you.
High-risk windows: missed doses, near the end of the monthly injection interval, and the weeks after discontinuation.
If relapse happens: treat it as data, not moral failure—re-engage care fast and reassess the treatment plan.
Naloxone planning: Patients with opioid use disorder (and their close contacts) should have access to naloxone or nalmefene and know how to use it.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing depends on the indication and the route (pill vs monthly injection). For opioid use disorder, starting is the tricky part: you must be opioid-free first to avoid precipitated withdrawal.

adult.aud_oral_initial: 25 mg PO once daily for several days (optional expert strategy) before increasing
adult.aud_oral_max: 100 mg PO once daily after at least 3 days based on response and tolerability
adult.aud_im: 380 mg IM (deep gluteal) once every 4 weeks
adult.oud_oral_induction: 25 mg PO once daily for 1 to 3 days; if no withdrawal signs occur, then 50 mg PO once daily thereafter (medically supervised initiation recommended)
adult.oud_im: 380 mg IM (deep gluteal) once every 4 weeks; if clinically wearing off before 4 weeks, some clinicians consider every 3 weeks (limited trial data for <4-week intervals)
adult.methamphetamine_use_disorder_off_label: 380 mg IM every 3 to 4 weeks when used as part of combination treatment (commonly paired with bupropion) in specialty addiction care
adult.opioid_free_requirement: Must be opioid-free (including tramadol) at least 7 to 10 days before starting; up to 14 days may be needed after long-acting opioids (e.g., methadone, buprenorphine). A naloxone challenge may be used when opioid-free status is uncertain.
adult.perioperative_discontinuation: If opioid pain management is anticipated: stop oral naltrexone at least 72 hours (3 days) before elective surgery; plan at least 30 days after the last IM injection (oral may be used temporarily if clinically appropriate).

sections.simple_explanation: Oral naltrexone is a daily pill that works best with strong routines or observed dosing when adherence is hard. Vivitrol is a monthly deep-IM injection that removes the daily decision but requires correct injection technique and long-range planning for surgeries or opioid pain needs.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Naltrexone can be used in select situations, but pregnancy and breastfeeding require careful risk-benefit decisions. For opioid use disorder in pregnancy, naltrexone is generally not the preferred first-line option.
sections.pregnancy: Naltrexone crosses the placenta. Data in pregnancy are limited. It is not typically the preferred medication for opioid use disorder during pregnancy, and extended-release IM naltrexone is generally avoided in pregnant patients in many guideline-based approaches. If a patient is stable on naltrexone and becomes pregnant, the decision to continue vs transition should be individualized based on relapse risk and patient preference, with shared decision-making and close monitoring. Pregnancy testing is commonly recommended before initiation.
sections.lactation: Naltrexone and its metabolite can be present in breast milk. The decision to breastfeed during therapy should weigh infant exposure risk, benefits of breastfeeding, and benefits of maternal treatment. For alcohol use disorder in breastfeeding patients, pharmacotherapy is generally used cautiously and typically not for routine management unless clearly needed (e.g., severe relapse risk), and non-pharmacologic supports are emphasized.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing. Older adults may have higher medical comorbidity burdens; monitor liver function, dizziness/syncope risk, and medication interactions closely.
sections.hepatic: Do not start during acute hepatitis or acute hepatic failure. In stable cirrhosis, some evidence-based guidance suggests no formal dose adjustment is required for oral or IM dosing, but clinical monitoring is critical. IM naltrexone avoids first-pass metabolism and may have more predictable exposure in liver impairment. If acute worsening of liver function occurs (e.g., hospitalization-level injury), consider interrupting therapy and resume only after resolution and reassessment.
sections.renal: Mild impairment: no adjustment typically needed. Moderate-to-severe impairment: use caution (limited study data); naltrexone and metabolite are primarily excreted in urine.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Liver function tests: baseline and periodic (especially in higher-risk patients: hepatitis C, HIV, ongoing heavy alcohol use, older age, higher oral doses, or other hepatotoxic meds).
Opioid-free status before initiation (OUD): verify opioid-free interval; consider naloxone challenge when there is doubt. Monitor closely during induction for precipitated withdrawal symptoms.
Mood monitoring: depression, irritability, suicidal thoughts—especially early in treatment or with comorbid mood disorders.
Injection-site checks (IM): pain, swelling, nodules are common; monitor for severe or worsening reactions (cellulitis, abscess, necrosis).
Overdose risk education: revisit at every visit—especially near end of injection interval, after missed doses, and if discontinuing treatment.
Pregnancy testing: baseline when clinically relevant and aligned with patient goals and guidelines in addiction care.
Infectious disease screening (commonly recommended in OUD care): hepatitis and HIV testing prior to initiation or early in treatment when not already known.
Adherence and engagement: oral naltrexone effectiveness collapses when adherence collapses—build a plan (routines, observed dosing, contingency management, supports).

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Naltrexone comes as a daily pill or a monthly injection. The choice is less about “which is stronger” and more about adherence, lifestyle, and medical planning (especially surgery/pain).
items: Oral tablets: 50 mg (commonly as naltrexone HCl; generics available)
IM extended-release injectable suspension (Vivitrol): 380 mg given once every 4 weeks (single-dose kit; deep IM gluteal only)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Naltrexone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist with the highest affinity for mu receptors. In opioid use disorder, it blocks the effects of opioids at the receptor level. In alcohol use disorder, blocking endogenous opioid signaling appears to reduce alcohol’s reinforcing “reward” effects and may also influence stress and craving pathways (including hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis effects).

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: For alcohol use disorder, naltrexone is a front-line medication option alongside therapy and behavior change support. For opioid use disorder, it’s an alternative to agonist treatments (buprenorphine or methadone) and is best suited for patients who can fully detox first and want a non-agonist approach. It can be a great fit when adherence is strong, the person is motivated, and there’s a solid plan for relapse risk and emergency overdose response.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: In psychiatry/addiction care, naltrexone is used for alcohol use disorder (to reduce cravings and heavy drinking) and opioid use disorder (to block opioid effects and reduce relapse risk after detox). It’s not a sedative and it’s not addictive.

faqs.q: Can I start naltrexone if I’m still drinking?
faqs.a: Yes, many clinicians start it while someone is still drinking. You don’t have to be abstinent first for alcohol use disorder. The bigger issue is making sure you’re not using opioids—because opioids plus naltrexone can trigger sudden withdrawal.

faqs.q: How long do I need to be opioid-free before starting?
faqs.a: Typically at least 7 to 10 days opioid-free (including tramadol). If you were on long-acting opioids like methadone or buprenorphine, some people need up to 14 days. When there’s any doubt, a supervised start and/or naloxone challenge can help confirm you’re truly opioid-free.

faqs.q: What happens if I take opioids while on naltrexone?
faqs.a: You may feel little to nothing because the receptors are blocked. The dangerous part is people trying to override the block by taking larger doses—that can cause overdose and death, especially as the medication wears off or after stopping when tolerance is lower.

faqs.q: Is Vivitrol stronger than oral naltrexone?
faqs.a: It’s not really about “stronger.” Vivitrol is long-acting and removes the daily pill decision, which can be a huge advantage. Oral naltrexone works well when adherence is strong. The best choice is usually the one you can realistically stick with.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Nausea is the classic one, especially early. Headache, dizziness, sleep problems, and anxiety/restlessness can happen too. With Vivitrol, injection-site reactions are common—anything severe, worsening, or associated with fever, drainage, or skin breakdown needs urgent evaluation.

It can. Depression and suicidal thoughts have been reported, including postmarketing reports. If mood gets darker, you feel hopeless, or you have suicidal thoughts, treat it like a real emergency and reach out immediately.

faqs.q: Is naltrexone hard on the liver?
faqs.a: It can raise liver enzymes, usually mildly and sometimes transiently. Rarely, more serious hepatitis-type injury has been reported. That’s why baseline and periodic liver tests are standard, and why clinicians avoid starting it during acute hepatitis or liver failure.

faqs.q: What if I need surgery or strong pain medication?
faqs.a: Plan ahead. If opioid pain meds might be needed, oral naltrexone is typically stopped at least 72 hours before elective surgery. With Vivitrol, you generally need about 30 days after the last injection for opioid responsiveness to return. Always tell surgeons, dentists, and ER clinicians you’re on naltrexone.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off naltrexone?
faqs.a: No taper is required. But stopping changes your risk profile—especially in opioid use disorder—because tolerance drops and overdose risk can rise if relapse occurs. If you stop, you should also have a clear relapse prevention plan and naloxone access if opioids are part of your history.

faqs.q: Can naltrexone be used for methamphetamine use disorder?
faqs.a: Sometimes off-label, usually as part of combination treatment in specialty addiction care (often paired with bupropion). It’s not a guaranteed fix, but it may provide modest benefit for some people when combined with therapy and structured support.
